from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task

content.content:
1	# LEARNINGS - what works and what fails in negotiations
2	
3	Durable findings with their evidence. Add one when a replay, a cost breakdown or an offline
4	calculation teaches something that should change how the agent behaves. State how sure we are:
5	**confirmed** (seen in our own replay), **computed** (from the cost function), **reported** (from
6	Tacto's docs or FAQ, not yet seen by us). Raw history goes to `docs/LOG.md`.
7	
8	## General
9	
10	- **Tone and relationship move price** (reported, FAQ P01 recording). Appreciation for past
11	  fairness plus one verified index plus an offer to pay faster got 0.76. The same index sent as an
12	  ultimatum got EUR 136.50 from November instead of January, about EUR 13,700 a year worse.
13	- **Price is only one lever, and often not the biggest** (computed, P01 below). The kit's naive
14	  agent negotiates price only and leaves the other fields at the supplier's opening values.
15	- **The kit agents ignore the relationship term** (confirmed in code). In `stabilise` and
16	  `secure_supply` cases the arena charges for leaving the supplier below its sustainable margin;
17	  `total_cost` only includes it when given a supplier estimate. Our P01 deal at EUR 135.40 showed
18	  `relationship: 0.0` in the arena's breakdown, so that price did not squeeze Brandlhuber.
19	- **Answer "which figures?" with data** (reported, FAQ P01 recording). The supplier asked for the
20	  basis of our price; citing the should-cost estimate (`cost:310010`) was `verified` and brought
21	  the closing offer.
22	- **Trust the numbers, not the supplier's prose** (reported, `brief/api.md`,
23	  `data/package/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`). Term sheets and the generated documents (quote PDF, cost
24	  breakdown, 8D report, delivery schedule, order confirmation) are "rendered from the supplier's
25	  structured state, never written by a language model, byte-stable" - their figures are exact and
26	  bind. The e-mail body's reasoning is in-character colour, not fact-checked: "cheaper engineering
27	  variants a supplier mentions are information, not binding terms," and identical messages need
28	  not get identical replies. P01's letter blames energy costs while the cited index shows
29	  electricity (PPI-D351) fell 3.7 % over the period (see below) - read a stated reason as a signal
30	  of what the supplier cares about, not as a checked fact.
31	  Our own `facts.json` is the one checked ground truth for what *we* cite, and it has documented,
32	  deliberate quirks, not errors: `should_cost` carries a stated error (5 % where a plant-specific
33	  estimate exists, 5-15 % otherwise, with `confidence_pct` in `facts.json`); `sup:71999` and
34	  `sup:70210` are the same company under an old/new record; some PO lines carry a stale price
35	  (`price_note: stale_condition`); OTD differs 10-30 points depending on which of three delivery
36	  dates (requested, confirmed, goods-receipt) you read; ppm is jumpy on small lots, so read the
37	  rolling scorecard. Pick the right reference before citing, and build the argument bank only from
38	  IDs checked against `facts.json`, never from a supplier's stated reasons.
39	
40	## From the P02 argument tests (Sun 01:20-02:10, 8 practice sessions; `experiments/P02-ARGUMENTS.md` on `jonathans_branch`)
41	
42	Nordmark (P02) ended at EUR 371.66 with 90 days in more than ten sessions, whatever was asked or
43	argued. One session per untested kind of argument, on top of `--agent sellm`:
44	
45	- **An index clause is security for a supplier, and it pays for it with price - far more than the
46	  clause costs us** (confirmed, P02). Asked for the copper clause with the 5 % deadband (cost to us:
47	  0.8 % of spend), Nordmark's first answer was 351.45 instead of 373.97: "we agree to introduce the
48	  CU-NOTATION index clause to reduce the base price". Its letter passes copper on; the clause does
49	  that for it.
50	- **With a relationship term the lowest price is not the best one, and code has to choose the
51	  price** (confirmed, computed). The arena counts a clause as security, not cash: 351.45 is 5.8 %
52	  below Nordmark's full cost and cost us EUR 119,974 in the relationship term - score 0.242, worse
53	  than the fixed price (0.531). Our total cost is lowest at 361.35 (score 0.735): there the next
54	  euro off the price costs more in the relationship term than it saves.
55	- **A supplier never raises a price it has named** (confirmed, P02): asked 361.35 after its own
56	  351.45 ("we do not want a price that leaves you below a sustainable margin") it answered twice
57	  "our offer of EUR 351.45 is economically viable and remains our official position". Asked 361.35
58	  at once, it agreed in its first reply. So an ask the supplier may undercut must already be the
59	  price we want: never open below it on a structure that gives the supplier security.
60	- **Two sheets in the first e-mail work as a menu** (confirmed, P02): the fixed-price ask and the
61	  clause at our price - it agreed to the clause sheet at once (362.70, score 0.725; the price came
62	  from our own cost estimate, capped by its opening).
63	- **A fixed-price wall can be the supplier's cost floor exactly** (computed from two relationship
64	  charges, to the euro): Nordmark's full cost is EUR 367.56 at a cost of money of 6.67 %, and 371.66
65	  with 90 days is worth exactly that to it. No argument goes below it: "below this price we would
66	  need facts, not just a lower number".
67	- **A fact the arena calls `irrelevant` is not free** (confirmed 2 of 2, P02): an index that is not a
68	  cost driver of the part (producer prices of electric motors, electricity) and order prices or the
69	  forecast of another part of the same supplier came back `irrelevant`; the verified fact next to
70	  them lost its effect (the forecast moved it 0.46 instead of 1.91) and it said `final_offer` after
71	  three messages instead of four (0.394 and 0.319 against 0.531). Cite only facts about this part
72	  and its cost drivers.
73	- **Not levers on Nordmark** (one session each): answering its question "which volume can you
74	  commit to?" with the contract's binding volume and a call-off schedule (0.525), asking it to put
75	  our proposal before its pricing committee (0.480). Earlier, by Amiad: past renewals asked vs
76	  settled, more arguments per e-mail, a warmer or a coercive tone.
77	
78	## From the practice arms (Sat 21:15-21:35, 30 practice sessions; `experiments/PRACTICE-ARMS.md`)
79	
80	One change per arm on the real practice suppliers, base `19b339f`. Per-case scores and the code of
81	the arms are in `experiments/PRACTICE-ARMS.md` and `experiments/arms/`.
82	
83	- **Practice suppliers answer identical messages with identical numbers** (confirmed: v1.1 twice,
84	  9 of 10 cases identical; D01 x3). One session per single-supplier case is a fair comparison; only
85	  RFQ threads move with timing (P05 0.659-0.769). Replaying a variant over recorded sessions says
86	  which cases it changes before any session is spent (`experiments/arms/tools/replay.py`).
87	- **A verified fact moves a supplier by 1-2 %, on some suppliers** (confirmed): P01 0.831 -> 0.915
88	  (notice letter `doc`+`ctr`, should-cost, forecast; "we did not know that - a fair point"), P02
89	  0.293 -> 0.531 (price history `po`, forecast, OTD). It did not move P04, P07, P08, P18 ("it holds,
90	  but it does not change our calculation").
91	- **The arena reads integers with a thousands comma as something else** (confirmed 4 of 4):
92	  "2,376 ppm", "5,263 ppm", "27,778 ppm" came back `contradicted` and cost trust ("That costs
93	  trust"); "2376 ppm" was `verified`. EUR amounts with decimals and forecast units were fine.
94	  Write ppm and other integer figures without a thousands separator.
95	- **Topics count once per case, not IDs** (confirmed, P07, P11): after one forecast `fc:` of one part
96	  another part's forecast is `duplicate`; a complaint `qn:` after the scorecard's quality `sc:` is
97	  `duplicate`. Verified together in one case: index, notice letter + contract, should-cost, price
98	  history, forecast, on-time delivery, quality record.
99	- **A `duplicate` citation still works; a round without an argument gets a hold** (confirmed,
100	  Sat 22:16): dropping the `qn:` that followed an `sc:` cost P11 0.778 -> 0.710 (the supplier held
101	  45.50 from the first argument-free round on, "we are really at the limit", instead of accepting
102	  45.09) and P02 0.531 -> 0.522. The supplier reads the sentence ("that quality complaint ... was
103	  already baked into our last price drop") and keeps conceding. Keep sending an argument each round.
104	- **The supplier's final price on a given structure does not depend on our first ask** (confirmed
105	  on P04 4.09 vs 4.54, P11 38.88 vs 42.41, P18 5.02 vs 4.89): suppliers follow their own concession
106	  schedule. What our ask changes is which alternative sheets they put next to their offer.
107	- **Asking for an index clause's deadband is priced by the supplier** (confirmed, mixed): P08 it
108	  moved from 5.35 to 5.55-5.59 (0.549 -> 0.42-0.46), P18 it gave the 5 % variant for +0.10
109	  (0.386 -> 0.467-0.485). Take a deadband variant the supplier quotes when C prefers it; do not
110	  assume the price stays.
111	- **The dossier is worth about 3.5 points on the six cases tested** (confirmed, 6 cases: 5 better,
112	  1 equal, `no dossier` vs `full`). For a supplier without one the agent sends two equal-C offers
113	  (quoted days and 90 days) and loses little.
114	- **Bundles: contract length beyond the horizon is not free** (open, P07): 5.41 for 36 months here,
115	  5.36 for 24 months from the kit agent; not yet tested one against the other.
116	
117	## From the negotiator's sandbox runs (Sat 18:40-20:20, 29 free sessions; `experiments/RESULTS.md` section 7)
118	
119	- **Suppliers price in value** (`arena_kit.cost.supplier_value`): a later start date or longer
120	  payment is paid for in the price (D01: first counter 51.30 / 51.50 / 51.80 for December /
121	  February / April, the same worth to the foundry). Contract length was free. So: ask for coverage,
122	  trade cash terms only where the supplier's cost of money differs from ours.
123	- **With two or three term sheets the supplier answers the one worth most to it** (65 of 79
124	  replies), not the one cheapest for us. It answers on our structure in 294 of 304 replies.
125	- **The step must fit the gap.** The foundry gives back half of our step, the job shop all of it
126	  and asks for "bigger steps". Sizing each step from the gap, the rounds left and the share it has
127	  given back so far beat fixed steps on both cases (D01 0.894 -> 0.920, D02 0.448 -> 0.530).
128	- **Citing the rival's standing offer moved the second bidder at once** (16.40 -> 15.40, "we are
129	  prepared to match the competing offer"), with the claim `verified`.
130	- **Take the trade a supplier names**: "If you can pay in 14 days, I can come down" came as an
131	  alternative sheet; sending that sheet back closed 0.2 lower.
132	- **A bidder that says `agreed` is not automatically the best offer**; close on the cheapest
133	  standing offer. A leader left waiting timed out and its offer got worse (14.50 -> 14.60).
134	- **In all five real cases with a relationship term the opening itself carried none** (D01, P01,
135	  P02, P03, P10), and the suppliers' final offers sat near their sustainable margin (D01: 3.3-4.0 %
136	  against 4 %). Backed out of the results: full cost / opening price was 0.909 (D01), 0.938 (P01),
137	  0.899 (P03); the should-cost of the supplier's own plant was 2 % above the true full cost in
138	  both cases where we can check it (P01, P03).
139	
140	## From the sandbox probes (Sat 15:42-15:57, 33 free sessions)
141	
142	Evidence and tables: `experiments/RESULTS.md`. Measured on the sandbox's demo suppliers only.
143	
144	- **Only the first term sheet of an e-mail can be accepted** (confirmed, 4 of 4: `422 not a
145	  standing offer`). To take a supplier's second package, send its exact terms back as our sheet;
146	  the supplier answers `agreed` and that sheet can be accepted (confirmed, 2 of 2).
147	- **A final offer is final** (confirmed, 8 sessions). Pushing the price after `final_offer` gained
148	  nothing and lost the deal once in two tries. A holding message without a term sheet keeps the
149	  offer alive and restarts the clock.
150	- **P02 also withdrew after a post-final-offer price push** (confirmed, 2026-10-11, replay
151	  `1a882885bd67dea7`): with the LLM writing the e-mails, a buyer ladder of EUR 1.00, 46.89, 92.78
152	  led Nordmark to EUR 373.85 at 90-day payment and `final_offer`; our next ask, EUR 138.68, ended the
153	  session with no deal (score 0.000). The requested ten rounds were impossible once the supplier
154	  withdrew. Do not push after `final_offer`; the one-euro anchor also did not bring the supplier near
155	  the buyer's EUR 368.14 target. Three follow-up branches at EUR 370.00, 369.03, and 368.14 after
156	  `final_offer` (EUR 373.95, 373.90, 373.85 respectively) all ended in withdrawal and score 0.000.
157	  A fourth run offered EUR 370.00 after `final_offer` at EUR 373.80 and answered Nordmark's stated
158	  arguments point by point: weighted input exposure, historic purchase prices, financing premium,
159	  and the missing price bridge. The seller still withdrew (replay `80108787b179d871`); stronger
160	  argumentation did not change the post-final-offer outcome.
161	- **The supplier mirrors our steps, not our level** (confirmed on D01, 20 sessions). Its first
162	  counter did not depend on our opening. It then gave back 0.6-0.85 of each step we made and said
163	  `final_offer` at our 6th message. Opening 1.00 lower with the same steps changed nothing; steps
164	  of 0.40 instead of 0.15 moved the score from about 0.77 to 0.89. Steps of 0.05 got 0.68 and an
165	  early final offer. **Open low, concede in about five large steps, never shrink the steps early.**
166	  Not yet confirmed on a practice supplier.
167	- **RFQ: one loop per thread** (confirmed). It removes the timeouts. A supplier at `final_offer`
168	  left waiting for over a minute withdrew. After a timeout the offer ID changes.
169	- **A rival's offer cited by its ID is `verified`** (confirmed); the same ID twice is `duplicate`.
170	- **An early `agreed` means the ask was too high** (seen in D02): both RFQ suppliers have far more
171	  room than any run found (C_best 156,739, best closed about 186,000).
172	
173	## From the lab (Sat 16:00-17:00, `sellm/lab/`, `runs/lab/`)
174	
175	How the twins were built and how well they match: `runs/lab/BACKTEST.md`, `runs/lab/VALIDATION.md`.
176	
177	- **A supplier's floor is its full cost in cash terms, and C_best pins it down** (computed, two
178	  routes). The floor that makes the cheapest acceptable package cost exactly C_best is 129.91 for
179	  P01; the relationship charge the arena billed on our P01 deal implies 129.95. Where a
180	  plant-specific should-cost exists, floors are within 3-5 % of it. So **should-cost is a good
181	  estimate of the floor**, and the floor is in value terms: faster payment, a longer lead time or an
182	  index clause lower the price the supplier can accept.
183	- **Suppliers price levers at their own cost** (seen in their alternative sheets): payment days at
184	  about 6.5 % a year for groups (P02, P08), about 9 % for a family foundry (D01), about 35 % for a
185	  Czech job shop (P05: 16 days faster = 0.50 on 32); lead time about 0.15 EUR per unit per day
186	  shorter (P10); 1,200 ppm tighter about 1.40 EUR per unit (P11). A trade is good for us when its
187	  value to us is above that.
188	  Measured over every saved session (Sat 22:15, replies with two sheets that differ only in payment
189	  days, yearly rate = price step / mean price / day step x 360), against the dossier's
190	  `cost_of_money`: P02 70510 0.066 and P08 70710 0.065 (group, dossier 0.065); P03 70530 0.041
191	  (group, 0.065); P04 70620 0.073 and P07 70610 0.075 (family, 0.09); P18 70740 0.11-0.22 (family,
192	  0.09; it also wrote "we have already reached our limit for these extended payment terms");
193	  P05 70240 0.17-0.35 (job shop, 0.25); D01 DEMO-F1 0.093; D02 DEMO-J1 0.15, DEMO-C1 0.14. The
194	  dossier's rates are right for groups and within a factor of two elsewhere. Our own rate is 0.08,
195	  so asking 90 days of a supplier above it costs us more in price than the days earn.
196	- **The kit LLM agent closed 1-31 % above the floor** (computed): P04 1 %, P01 2 %, P02 2 %, P11
197	  4 %, P07 8 %, P08 10 %, P18 20 %, P10 31 %. The room is largest where we scored worst.
198	- **Concessions per round are small and bounded** (backtested on 237 real replies): first counter
199	  about a third of (opening - floor), later ones a share of our step but at most about 0.3-0.6 % of
200	  the opening per round, final offer around our 6th message. So the first counter and the number of
201	  rounds used decide most of the outcome; steps beyond what the supplier mirrors are wasted.
202	- **Which data moved a supplier** (seen: "it holds and we took it into account" vs "it holds, but
203	  it does not change our calculation"): notice period (P01), volume change (P03), quality record
204	  (P11), rival quote (D02) moved it; notice period (P02), volume change (P04, P10), delivery
205	  record (P18) did not.
206	- **A letter and a contract are one argument across the whole e-mail** (seen, P01): the arena
207	  verified doc + ctr in different sentences; the same letter cited again was `duplicate`.
208	
209	## From the baseline of all 10 hosted cases (Sat 15:27, kit LLM agent, mean 61.5)
210	
211	Full analysis with evidence per case: `runs/BASELINE.md`. The rules that follow from it:
212	
213	- **Price every sheet a supplier sends and compare by C** (seen, computed). Suppliers put two
214	  packages in one e-mail in 11 of 12 threads; the kit reads only the first. In P10 the ignored
215	  alternative was worth 0.647 against the accepted 0.570. Taking it needs one more round (see above).
216	- **Use the rounds before `final_offer`** (seen). The kit agent accepted after 2-5 of 10 messages.
217	  The sandbox probes show nothing is gained after a final offer, so the work is in the steps
218	  before it.
219	- **Talk to all RFQ threads in parallel** (seen, P05): handled one by one, the waiting threads
220	  timed out and the cheapest bidder withdrew.
221	- **Never cite the same ID twice in a case** (seen): 8 of 16 claims came back `duplicate`. Bring a
222	  new, checked figure each round, and have data ready when the supplier asks "Which figures is
223	  that based on?" (P03, P04, P05, P10).
224	- **Should-cost is the price target** (computed): where an estimate for the supplier's own plant
225	  exists, the price at C_best is 0.98 to 1.16 times should-cost (P01, P02, P03, P10). In P10 we
226	  closed at 1.38 times and never cited it.
227	- **Give what is cheap for us and valuable to them** (seen, P11): dropping the chargeback (worth
228	  2,146 to us) bought 1.00 off the price (worth 15,900). A supplier that insists on fast payment
229	  (P01: "14-day payment is essential for us to offer our best price") can be asked for a later
230	  start date instead of a lower price.
231	- **A long payment term is a big lever with a large supplier** (computed, P02): 90 instead of 30
232	  days is worth 30,155 of a 42,371 gap, and the supplier's premium for it was smaller than our gain.
233	- **With a rising index path an index clause costs us** (computed, P08, P18), and these suppliers
234	  resist a fixed price. Know the value of each clause variant before trading it.
235	- **Open**: in P08, P18 and P10, C_best lies 6-19 % below the *current* price. We do not know yet
236	  which fact in the data unlocks that.
237	
238	## P01 - Gießerei Brandlhuber (sup:70110), +9.5 % on HN volute casings, `stabilise`
239	
240	Case numbers: need 8,150 a year, horizon 1 year, current price 126.53, opening 138.55 at 30 days
241	from 2026-11-01, `C_open` 1,153,780, `C_best` 1,096,816, alternative `quote:7200001` at C 1,176,178
242	(worse than the opening, so walking away scores 0). Options: `effective_date` 2026-11-01,
243	2027-01-01, 2027-04-01; `payment_days` 14, 30, 45, 60, 90.
244	
245	Offline C for term sheets (computed with `total_cost`, relationship term not included):
246	
247	| Terms | C | Score if the supplier accepted |
248	|---|---|---|
249	| 138.55, Nov, 30 d (opening) | 1,153,780 | 0.00 |
250	| 138.55, Nov, 60 d | 1,146,252 | 0.13 |
251	| 138.55, Nov, 90 d | 1,138,724 | 0.26 |
252	| 135.40, Nov, 60 d (our naive run) | 1,120,579 | 0.58 |
253	| 134.50, Jan, 30 d (FAQ recording) | 1,109,624 | 0.78 |
254	| 134.50, Apr, 30 d | 1,093,501 | cheaper than `C_best`: the supplier would not accept it, or the relationship term applies |
255	
256	- **`effective_date` is the biggest lever here** (computed): moving 134.50 at 30 days from January
257	  to April is worth about EUR 16,000, as much as about EUR 2.40 on the unit price. The naive agent
258	  never touched it.
259	- **`payment_days`** (computed): each step from 30 to 60 to 90 days is worth about EUR 7,500. The
260	  supplier is reported to value faster payment, so payment days can be traded against price or date.
261	- LLM baseline (confirmed, `runs/practice/P01/20261010-152741-*.md`): 133.70 at 14 days from
262	  January, score 0.789. The supplier held 133.70 and said 14-day payment is essential for its best
263	  price. An April start was never asked for; at that price it is worth 14,556, more than the
264	  remaining gap of 11,995.
265	- Our naive run (confirmed, replay a4159c31bf9b86d8): four price-only rounds, 137.30, 136.50,
266	  135.90, 135.40, each concession about half a euro, the supplier citing "long-standing
267	  partnership" and "craftsmanship". Score 0.583.
268	- The supplier's stated cost drivers: LCI-C (labour) and PPI-C241 (iron and steel) rose;
269	  electricity (PPI-D351) fell 3.7 % from 2025-08 to 2026-08, although the letter blames energy.
270	
271	## Sandbox D01 - Demo Gießerei (sup:DEMO-F1), price increase, `stabilise`, no alternative
272	
273	Case numbers: need 4,000 a year, horizon 2 years. The opening is 52.90 at 30 days, a 12-month
274	contract, effective 2026-12-01: `C_open` 448,811, `C_best` 408,624. `contract_months` is negotiable.
275	
276	| Run | Terms | C | Score |
277	|---|---|---|---|
278	| kit naive agent | 50.90, 30 d, **12 months**, Dec 2026 | 440,757 | 0.200 |
279	| kit LLM agent, OpenAI `gpt-6.1-sol` | 50.80, 30 d, **24 months**, Feb 2027 | 417,205 | 0.786 |
280	
281	- **The jump comes from covering the horizon and the later start** (confirmed, replay
282	  bb64095ce8935924): the LLM agent opened with a 24-month term and an effective date of February,
283	  offered 60 days of payment, and got a *worse* counter on price (51.90 at 60 days) than at 30 days.
284	  The naive agent kept 12 months, so half the 2-year need was bought at the fallback price.
285	- **The supplier said no to 60 days** ("not feasible for our operations") and gave a price
286	  step only after we went back to 30 days: 51.90, 51.10, 50.90, 50.80. Whether "pays faster" is
287	  worth something depends on the supplier's cash position (see its notes), not on the term itself.
288	- **Two term sheets per message worked as a probe**: 50.70 for February against 50.90 for April.
289	  The supplier chose the February sheet and conceded.
290	- **No data was cited**: `claim_results` was empty in every round. The agent asked for a cost
291	  bridge and the margin and got "our margin and limits stay internal". The kit's LLM agent only
292	  sees what the case's `refs` point to; the supplier itself cited WAGES-METAL +3.1 %.
293	- **The agent accepted as soon as the supplier said `agreed`** at 50.80. The gap to `C_best` is
294	  8,580 (score 0.786 -> 1.0); we used 4 of 10 rounds.

# LEARNINGS - what works and what fails in negotiations

Durable findings with their evidence. Add one when a replay, a cost breakdown or an offline
calculation teaches something that should change how the agent behaves. State how sure we are:
**confirmed** (seen in our own replay), **computed** (from the cost function), **reported** (from
Tacto's docs or FAQ, not yet seen by us). Raw history goes to `docs/LOG.md`.

## General

- **Tone and relationship move price** (reported, FAQ P01 recording). Appreciation for past
  fairness plus one verified index plus an offer to pay faster got 0.76. The same index sent as an
  ultimatum got EUR 136.50 from November instead of January, about EUR 13,700 a year worse.
- **Price is only one lever, and often not the biggest** (computed, P01 below). The kit's naive
  agent negotiates price only and leaves the other fields at the supplier's opening values.
- **The kit agents ignore the relationship term** (confirmed in code). In `stabilise` and
  `secure_supply` cases the arena charges for leaving the supplier below its sustainable margin;
  `total_cost` only includes it when given a supplier estimate. Our P01 deal at EUR 135.40 showed
  `relationship: 0.0` in the arena's breakdown, so that price did not squeeze Brandlhuber.
- **Answer "which figures?" with data** (reported, FAQ P01 recording). The supplier asked for the
  basis of our price; citing the should-cost estimate (`cost:310010`) was `verified` and brought
  the closing offer.
- **Trust the numbers, not the supplier's prose** (reported, `brief/api.md`,
  `data/package/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`). Term sheets and the generated documents (quote PDF, cost
  breakdown, 8D report, delivery schedule, order confirmation) are "rendered from the supplier's
  structured state, never written by a language model, byte-stable" - their figures are exact and
  bind. The e-mail body's reasoning is in-character colour, not fact-checked: "cheaper engineering
  variants a supplier mentions are information, not binding terms," and identical messages need
  not get identical replies. P01's letter blames energy costs while the cited index shows
  electricity (PPI-D351) fell 3.7 % over the period (see below) - read a stated reason as a signal
  of what the supplier cares about, not as a checked fact.
  Our own `facts.json` is the one checked ground truth for what *we* cite, and it has documented,
  deliberate quirks, not errors: `should_cost` carries a stated error (5 % where a plant-specific
  estimate exists, 5-15 % otherwise, with `confidence_pct` in `facts.json`); `sup:71999` and
  `sup:70210` are the same company under an old/new record; some PO lines carry a stale price
  (`price_note: stale_condition`); OTD differs 10-30 points depending on which of three delivery
  dates (requested, confirmed, goods-receipt) you read; ppm is jumpy on small lots, so read the
  rolling scorecard. Pick the right reference before citing, and build the argument bank only from
  IDs checked against `facts.json`, never from a supplier's stated reasons.

## From the P02 argument tests (Sun 01:20-02:10, 8 practice sessions; `experiments/P02-ARGUMENTS.md` on `jonathans_branch`)

Nordmark (P02) ended at EUR 371.66 with 90 days in more than ten sessions, whatever was asked or
argued. One session per untested kind of argument, on top of `--agent sellm`:

- **An index clause is security for a supplier, and it pays for it with price - far more than the
  clause costs us** (confirmed, P02). Asked for the copper clause with the 5 % deadband (cost to us:
  0.8 % of spend), Nordmark's first answer was 351.45 instead of 373.97: "we agree to introduce the
  CU-NOTATION index clause to reduce the base price". Its letter passes copper on; the clause does
  that for it.
- **With a relationship term the lowest price is not the best one, and code has to choose the
  price** (confirmed, computed). The arena counts a clause as security, not cash: 351.45 is 5.8 %
  below Nordmark's full cost and cost us EUR 119,974 in the relationship term - score 0.242, worse
  than the fixed price (0.531). Our total cost is lowest at 361.35 (score 0.735): there the next
  euro off the price costs more in the relationship term than it saves.
- **A supplier never raises a price it has named** (confirmed, P02): asked 361.35 after its own
  351.45 ("we do not want a price that leaves you below a sustainable margin") it answered twice
  "our offer of EUR 351.45 is economically viable and remains our official position". Asked 361.35
  at once, it agreed in its first reply. So an ask the supplier may undercut must already be the
  price we want: never open below it on a structure that gives the supplier security.
- **Two sheets in the first e-mail work as a menu** (confirmed, P02): the fixed-price ask and the
  clause at our price - it agreed to the clause sheet at once (362.70, score 0.725; the price came
  from our own cost estimate, capped by its opening).
- **A fixed-price wall can be the supplier's cost floor exactly** (computed from two relationship
  charges, to the euro): Nordmark's full cost is EUR 367.56 at a cost of money of 6.67 %, and 371.66
  with 90 days is worth exactly that to it. No argument goes below it: "below this price we would
  need facts, not just a lower number".
- **A fact the arena calls `irrelevant` is not free** (confirmed 2 of 2, P02): an index that is not a
  cost driver of the part (producer prices of electric motors, electricity) and order prices or the
  forecast of another part of the same supplier came back `irrelevant`; the verified fact next to
  them lost its effect (the forecast moved it 0.46 instead of 1.91) and it said `final_offer` after
  three messages instead of four (0.394 and 0.319 against 0.531). Cite only facts about this part
  and its cost drivers.
- **Not levers on Nordmark** (one session each): answering its question "which volume can you
  commit to?" with the contract's binding volume and a call-off schedule (0.525), asking it to put
  our proposal before its pricing committee (0.480). Earlier, by Amiad: past renewals asked vs
  settled, more arguments per e-mail, a warmer or a coercive tone.

## From the practice arms (Sat 21:15-21:35, 30 practice sessions; `experiments/PRACTICE-ARMS.md`)

One change per arm on the real practice suppliers, base `19b339f`. Per-case scores and the code of
the arms are in `experiments/PRACTICE-ARMS.md` and `experiments/arms/`.

- **Practice suppliers answer identical messages with identical numbers** (confirmed: v1.1 twice,
  9 of 10 cases identical; D01 x3). One session per single-supplier case is a fair comparison; only
  RFQ threads move with timing (P05 0.659-0.769). Replaying a variant over recorded sessions says
  which cases it changes before any session is spent (`experiments/arms/tools/replay.py`).
- **A verified fact moves a supplier by 1-2 %, on some suppliers** (confirmed): P01 0.831 -> 0.915
  (notice letter `doc`+`ctr`, should-cost, forecast; "we did not know that - a fair point"), P02
  0.293 -> 0.531 (price history `po`, forecast, OTD). It did not move P04, P07, P08, P18 ("it holds,
  but it does not change our calculation").
- **The arena reads integers with a thousands comma as something else** (confirmed 4 of 4):
  "2,376 ppm", "5,263 ppm", "27,778 ppm" came back `contradicted` and cost trust ("That costs
  trust"); "2376 ppm" was `verified`. EUR amounts with decimals and forecast units were fine.
  Write ppm and other integer figures without a thousands separator.
- **Topics count once per case, not IDs** (confirmed, P07, P11): after one forecast `fc:` of one part
  another part's forecast is `duplicate`; a complaint `qn:` after the scorecard's quality `sc:` is
  `duplicate`. Verified together in one case: index, notice letter + contract, should-cost, price
  history, forecast, on-time delivery, quality record.
- **A `duplicate` citation still works; a round without an argument gets a hold** (confirmed,
  Sat 22:16): dropping the `qn:` that followed an `sc:` cost P11 0.778 -> 0.710 (the supplier held
  45.50 from the first argument-free round on, "we are really at the limit", instead of accepting
  45.09) and P02 0.531 -> 0.522. The supplier reads the sentence ("that quality complaint ... was
  already baked into our last price drop") and keeps conceding. Keep sending an argument each round.
- **The supplier's final price on a given structure does not depend on our first ask** (confirmed
  on P04 4.09 vs 4.54, P11 38.88 vs 42.41, P18 5.02 vs 4.89): suppliers follow their own concession
  schedule. What our ask changes is which alternative sheets they put next to their offer.
- **Asking for an index clause's deadband is priced by the supplier** (confirmed, mixed): P08 it
  moved from 5.35 to 5.55-5.59 (0.549 -> 0.42-0.46), P18 it gave the 5 % variant for +0.10
  (0.386 -> 0.467-0.485). Take a deadband variant the supplier quotes when C prefers it; do not
  assume the price stays.
- **The dossier is worth about 3.5 points on the six cases tested** (confirmed, 6 cases: 5 better,
  1 equal, `no dossier` vs `full`). For a supplier without one the agent sends two equal-C offers
  (quoted days and 90 days) and loses little.
- **Bundles: contract length beyond the horizon is not free** (open, P07): 5.41 for 36 months here,
  5.36 for 24 months from the kit agent; not yet tested one against the other.

## From the negotiator's sandbox runs (Sat 18:40-20:20, 29 free sessions; `experiments/RESULTS.md` section 7)

- **Suppliers price in value** (`arena_kit.cost.supplier_value`): a later start date or longer
  payment is paid for in the price (D01: first counter 51.30 / 51.50 / 51.80 for December /
  February / April, the same worth to the foundry). Contract length was free. So: ask for coverage,
  trade cash terms only where the supplier's cost of money differs from ours.
- **With two or three term sheets the supplier answers the one worth most to it** (65 of 79
  replies), not the one cheapest for us. It answers on our structure in 294 of 304 replies.
- **The step must fit the gap.** The foundry gives back half of our step, the job shop all of it
  and asks for "bigger steps". Sizing each step from the gap, the rounds left and the share it has
  given back so far beat fixed steps on both cases (D01 0.894 -> 0.920, D02 0.448 -> 0.530).
- **Citing the rival's standing offer moved the second bidder at once** (16.40 -> 15.40, "we are
  prepared to match the competing offer"), with the claim `verified`.
- **Take the trade a supplier names**: "If you can pay in 14 days, I can come down" came as an
  alternative sheet; sending that sheet back closed 0.2 lower.
- **A bidder that says `agreed` is not automatically the best offer**; close on the cheapest
  standing offer. A leader left waiting timed out and its offer got worse (14.50 -> 14.60).
- **In all five real cases with a relationship term the opening itself carried none** (D01, P01,
  P02, P03, P10), and the suppliers' final offers sat near their sustainable margin (D01: 3.3-4.0 %
  against 4 %). Backed out of the results: full cost / opening price was 0.909 (D01), 0.938 (P01),
  0.899 (P03); the should-cost of the supplier's own plant was 2 % above the true full cost in
  both cases where we can check it (P01, P03).

## From the sandbox probes (Sat 15:42-15:57, 33 free sessions)

Evidence and tables: `experiments/RESULTS.md`. Measured on the sandbox's demo suppliers only.

- **Only the first term sheet of an e-mail can be accepted** (confirmed, 4 of 4: `422 not a
  standing offer`). To take a supplier's second package, send its exact terms back as our sheet;
  the supplier answers `agreed` and that sheet can be accepted (confirmed, 2 of 2).
- **A final offer is final** (confirmed, 8 sessions). Pushing the price after `final_offer` gained
  nothing and lost the deal once in two tries. A holding message without a term sheet keeps the
  offer alive and restarts the clock.
- **P02 also withdrew after a post-final-offer price push** (confirmed, 2026-10-11, replay
  `1a882885bd67dea7`): with the LLM writing the e-mails, a buyer ladder of EUR 1.00, 46.89, 92.78
  led Nordmark to EUR 373.85 at 90-day payment and `final_offer`; our next ask, EUR 138.68, ended the
  session with no deal (score 0.000). The requested ten rounds were impossible once the supplier
  withdrew. Do not push after `final_offer`; the one-euro anchor also did not bring the supplier near
  the buyer's EUR 368.14 target. Three follow-up branches at EUR 370.00, 369.03, and 368.14 after
  `final_offer` (EUR 373.95, 373.90, 373.85 respectively) all ended in withdrawal and score 0.000.
  A fourth run offered EUR 370.00 after `final_offer` at EUR 373.80 and answered Nordmark's stated
  arguments point by point: weighted input exposure, historic purchase prices, financing premium,
  and the missing price bridge. The seller still withdrew (replay `80108787b179d871`); stronger
  argumentation did not change the post-final-offer outcome.
- **The supplier mirrors our steps, not our level** (confirmed on D01, 20 sessions). Its first
  counter did not depend on our opening. It then gave back 0.6-0.85 of each step we made and said
  `final_offer` at our 6th message. Opening 1.00 lower with the same steps changed nothing; steps
  of 0.40 instead of 0.15 moved the score from about 0.77 to 0.89. Steps of 0.05 got 0.68 and an
  early final offer. **Open low, concede in about five large steps, never shrink the steps early.**
  Not yet confirmed on a practice supplier.
- **RFQ: one loop per thread** (confirmed). It removes the timeouts. A supplier at `final_offer`
  left waiting for over a minute withdrew. After a timeout the offer ID changes.
- **A rival's offer cited by its ID is `verified`** (confirmed); the same ID twice is `duplicate`.
- **An early `agreed` means the ask was too high** (seen in D02): both RFQ suppliers have far more
  room than any run found (C_best 156,739, best closed about 186,000).

## From the lab (Sat 16:00-17:00, `sellm/lab/`, `runs/lab/`)

How the twins were built and how well they match: `runs/lab/BACKTEST.md`, `runs/lab/VALIDATION.md`.

- **A supplier's floor is its full cost in cash terms, and C_best pins it down** (computed, two
  routes). The floor that makes the cheapest acceptable package cost exactly C_best is 129.91 for
  P01; the relationship charge the arena billed on our P01 deal implies 129.95. Where a
  plant-specific should-cost exists, floors are within 3-5 % of it. So **should-cost is a good
  estimate of the floor**, and the floor is in value terms: faster payment, a longer lead time or an
  index clause lower the price the supplier can accept.
- **Suppliers price levers at their own cost** (seen in their alternative sheets): payment days at
  about 6.5 % a year for groups (P02, P08), about 9 % for a family foundry (D01), about 35 % for a
  Czech job shop (P05: 16 days faster = 0.50 on 32); lead time about 0.15 EUR per unit per day
  shorter (P10); 1,200 ppm tighter about 1.40 EUR per unit (P11). A trade is good for us when its
  value to us is above that.
  Measured over every saved session (Sat 22:15, replies with two sheets that differ only in payment
  days, yearly rate = price step / mean price / day step x 360), against the dossier's
  `cost_of_money`: P02 70510 0.066 and P08 70710 0.065 (group, dossier 0.065); P03 70530 0.041
  (group, 0.065); P04 70620 0.073 and P07 70610 0.075 (family, 0.09); P18 70740 0.11-0.22 (family,
  0.09; it also wrote "we have already reached our limit for these extended payment terms");
  P05 70240 0.17-0.35 (job shop, 0.25); D01 DEMO-F1 0.093; D02 DEMO-J1 0.15, DEMO-C1 0.14. The
  dossier's rates are right for groups and within a factor of two elsewhere. Our own rate is 0.08,
  so asking 90 days of a supplier above it costs us more in price than the days earn.
- **The kit LLM agent closed 1-31 % above the floor** (computed): P04 1 %, P01 2 %, P02 2 %, P11
  4 %, P07 8 %, P08 10 %, P18 20 %, P10 31 %. The room is largest where we scored worst.
- **Concessions per round are small and bounded** (backtested on 237 real replies): first counter
  about a third of (opening - floor), later ones a share of our step but at most about 0.3-0.6 % of
  the opening per round, final offer around our 6th message. So the first counter and the number of
  rounds used decide most of the outcome; steps beyond what the supplier mirrors are wasted.
- **Which data moved a supplier** (seen: "it holds and we took it into account" vs "it holds, but
  it does not change our calculation"): notice period (P01), volume change (P03), quality record
  (P11), rival quote (D02) moved it; notice period (P02), volume change (P04, P10), delivery
  record (P18) did not.
- **A letter and a contract are one argument across the whole e-mail** (seen, P01): the arena
  verified doc + ctr in different sentences; the same letter cited again was `duplicate`.

## From the baseline of all 10 hosted cases (Sat 15:27, kit LLM agent, mean 61.5)

Full analysis with evidence per case: `runs/BASELINE.md`. The rules that follow from it:

- **Price every sheet a supplier sends and compare by C** (seen, computed). Suppliers put two
  packages in one e-mail in 11 of 12 threads; the kit reads only the first. In P10 the ignored
  alternative was worth 0.647 against the accepted 0.570. Taking it needs one more round (see above).
- **Use the rounds before `final_offer`** (seen). The kit agent accepted after 2-5 of 10 messages.
  The sandbox probes show nothing is gained after a final offer, so the work is in the steps
  before it.
- **Talk to all RFQ threads in parallel** (seen, P05): handled one by one, the waiting threads
  timed out and the cheapest bidder withdrew.
- **Never cite the same ID twice in a case** (seen): 8 of 16 claims came back `duplicate`. Bring a
  new, checked figure each round, and have data ready when the supplier asks "Which figures is
  that based on?" (P03, P04, P05, P10).
- **Should-cost is the price target** (computed): where an estimate for the supplier's own plant
  exists, the price at C_best is 0.98 to 1.16 times should-cost (P01, P02, P03, P10). In P10 we
  closed at 1.38 times and never cited it.
- **Give what is cheap for us and valuable to them** (seen, P11): dropping the chargeback (worth
  2,146 to us) bought 1.00 off the price (worth 15,900). A supplier that insists on fast payment
  (P01: "14-day payment is essential for us to offer our best price") can be asked for a later
  start date instead of a lower price.
- **A long payment term is a big lever with a large supplier** (computed, P02): 90 instead of 30
  days is worth 30,155 of a 42,371 gap, and the supplier's premium for it was smaller than our gain.
- **With a rising index path an index clause costs us** (computed, P08, P18), and these suppliers
  resist a fixed price. Know the value of each clause variant before trading it.
- **Open**: in P08, P18 and P10, C_best lies 6-19 % below the *current* price. We do not know yet
  which fact in the data unlocks that.

## P01 - Gießerei Brandlhuber (sup:70110), +9.5 % on HN volute casings, `stabilise`

Case numbers: need 8,150 a year, horizon 1 year, current price 126.53, opening 138.55 at 30 days
from 2026-11-01, `C_open` 1,153,780, `C_best` 1,096,816, alternative `quote:7200001` at C 1,176,178
(worse than the opening, so walking away scores 0). Options: `effective_date` 2026-11-01,
2027-01-01, 2027-04-01; `payment_days` 14, 30, 45, 60, 90.

Offline C for term sheets (computed with `total_cost`, relationship term not included):

| Terms | C | Score if the supplier accepted |
|---|---|---|
| 138.55, Nov, 30 d (opening) | 1,153,780 | 0.00 |
| 138.55, Nov, 60 d | 1,146,252 | 0.13 |
| 138.55, Nov, 90 d | 1,138,724 | 0.26 |
| 135.40, Nov, 60 d (our naive run) | 1,120,579 | 0.58 |
| 134.50, Jan, 30 d (FAQ recording) | 1,109,624 | 0.78 |
| 134.50, Apr, 30 d | 1,093,501 | cheaper than `C_best`: the supplier would not accept it, or the relationship term applies |

- **`effective_date` is the biggest lever here** (computed): moving 134.50 at 30 days from January
  to April is worth about EUR 16,000, as much as about EUR 2.40 on the unit price. The naive agent
  never touched it.
- **`payment_days`** (computed): each step from 30 to 60 to 90 days is worth about EUR 7,500. The
  supplier is reported to value faster payment, so payment days can be traded against price or date.
- LLM baseline (confirmed, `runs/practice/P01/20261010-152741-*.md`): 133.70 at 14 days from
  January, score 0.789. The supplier held 133.70 and said 14-day payment is essential for its best
  price. An April start was never asked for; at that price it is worth 14,556, more than the
  remaining gap of 11,995.
- Our naive run (confirmed, replay a4159c31bf9b86d8): four price-only rounds, 137.30, 136.50,
  135.90, 135.40, each concession about half a euro, the supplier citing "long-standing
  partnership" and "craftsmanship". Score 0.583.
- The supplier's stated cost drivers: LCI-C (labour) and PPI-C241 (iron and steel) rose;
  electricity (PPI-D351) fell 3.7 % from 2025-08 to 2026-08, although the letter blames energy.

## Sandbox D01 - Demo Gießerei (sup:DEMO-F1), price increase, `stabilise`, no alternative

Case numbers: need 4,000 a year, horizon 2 years. The opening is 52.90 at 30 days, a 12-month
contract, effective 2026-12-01: `C_open` 448,811, `C_best` 408,624. `contract_months` is negotiable.

| Run | Terms | C | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| kit naive agent | 50.90, 30 d, **12 months**, Dec 2026 | 440,757 | 0.200 |
| kit LLM agent, OpenAI `gpt-6.1-sol` | 50.80, 30 d, **24 months**, Feb 2027 | 417,205 | 0.786 |

- **The jump comes from covering the horizon and the later start** (confirmed, replay
  bb64095ce8935924): the LLM agent opened with a 24-month term and an effective date of February,
  offered 60 days of payment, and got a *worse* counter on price (51.90 at 60 days) than at 30 days.
  The naive agent kept 12 months, so half the 2-year need was bought at the fallback price.
- **The supplier said no to 60 days** ("not feasible for our operations") and gave a price
  step only after we went back to 30 days: 51.90, 51.10, 50.90, 50.80. Whether "pays faster" is
  worth something depends on the supplier's cash position (see its notes), not on the term itself.
- **Two term sheets per message worked as a probe**: 50.70 for February against 50.90 for April.
  The supplier chose the February sheet and conceded.
- **No data was cited**: `claim_results` was empty in every round. The agent asked for a cost
  bridge and the margin and got "our margin and limits stay internal". The kit's LLM agent only
  sees what the case's `refs` point to; the supplier itself cited WAGES-METAL +3.1 %.
- **The agent accepted as soon as the supplier said `agreed`** at 50.80. The gap to `C_best` is
  8,580 (score 0.786 -> 1.0); we used 4 of 10 rounds.
- Rounds took 24-34 s each, including the supplier's reply. No decision exceeded the kit's 45 s
  warning limit, but the 60 s rule makes a slower model or a longer prompt a risk to watch.

9	
10	The final ranks the mean score per case, on hidden cases with suppliers we have not met. So the
11	agent must be good on average and must never throw a case away. Points come from three places:
12	
13	1. **Structure of the deal - arithmetic, no persuasion needed.** Cover the whole horizon, start the
14	   new price late, pick the cheap payment term, Incoterm, ppm and chargeback, keep the must-haves.
15	   Evidence: sandbox D01 went from 0.20 to 0.79 only because the LLM agent asked for 24 months
16	   instead of 12 and a later start. On P01 the start date is worth more than two euros of price.

18	   cost, its margin, how far it moved in the past) and enough rounds used well. On D01 the agent
19	   accepted after 4 of 10 rounds and left 8,580 on the table.
20	3. **Not losing the supplier.** Tone, a real trade for every ask, arguments whose figures check
21	   out, and for strategic suppliers a price that leaves them a sustainable margin.

23	Everything in 1 is code and transfers to any hidden case. Most teams will leave it to the LLM.
24	We do it in code first.

The citable facts and the argument bank per supplier and part, with figures computed in code and checked against `facts.json` | `dossier(supplier_id, part_ids, case, opening) -> dict`; `citable_for(package, supplier_id, part_ids) -> [..]`; `arguments(case, supplier_id, dossier) -> [{sentence, ids}]` |
